Taking my own numbers at face value: a computerised flat produces ~12-25 garments'-worth of panels/machine/shift; a single linker joins ~20-45 sweaters/linker/shift. So at a 1:1 machine:linker ratio the linker is NOT strictly the bottleneck on the central estimates — the linker can roughly keep pace with or outpace one knitting machine. The honest reconciliation: linking becomes the binding ceiling as soon as knitting capacity is added or a machine's panel output sits at the top of its band while the linker sits at the bottom of its (e.g. a 25-panel machine against a 20-sweater linker), and more importantly the bands overlap so heavily that the two steps are roughly BALANCED at 1:1, which means (i) you cannot add knitting machines without adding linkers, and (ii) the linker is the step that is hardest to SCALE (hand skill, eyesight-intensive, piece-rate, T1's hardest-to-re-hire role) even where it is not numerically slower per shift. So the defensible claim is 'linking is the constraint that GOVERNS scaling and is the hard-to-add capacity' rather than 'a single linker is always numerically slower than a single knitting machine.' Correct framing: the bands support 'linking is A binding, hard-to-scale constraint requiring linker capacity to be matched to (and often exceed 1:1) knitting capacity,' NOT 'the bands prove one linker is slower than one machine.'

answers.grounded_in: machines.specialist.json glossary 'periphery-only reverse-engineering rule' + 'core kinematic chain' + conflicts_and_dominance[6] (periphery YES / core chain NEVER) + boundaries (never reverse-engineer needle bed, needles, cam systems, electronic needle-selection, controller firmware, knit-CAD); kb3 node PERIPHERY_REVERSE_ENG + KINEMATIC_CHAIN_WALL.
answers.answer: [ESTIMATE, MED — rule is directionally sound but under-operationalised] The honest answer is that my rule as written is largely TWO LISTS (core = needle bed / needles / cams / electronic needle-selection / controller firmware / knit-CAD = NEVER; periphery = jigs, fixtures, alignment gauges, non-critical spares, cam-timing LEARNING, scanning obsolete brackets = OK), and the question correctly presses whether those lists actually DECIDE the borderline cases. Let me supply the operational test the KB implies but does not state crisply. The decisive test is a conjunction: a part is PERIPHERY-safe to reverse-engineer/3D-print only if ALL hold — (i) it is NOT one of the named core-chain subsystems; (ii) it does NOT set or hold stitch-forming precision (bed flatness, gauge pitch, needle timing, cam profile geometry, yarn-path registration) — i.e. its dimensional tolerance does not feed the loop-formation metrology; (iii) failure of the part degrades convenience/maintenance, not stitch integrity or machine safety; (iv) it clones no firmware/knit-CAD IP. Applying it to the three borderline cases: (a) worn needle-bed ALIGNMENT GAUGE — this SETS/verifies bed flatness and gauge pitch, i.e. it is metrology feeding the core chain, so it FAILS test (ii): treat as CORE-adjacent, do NOT home-fabricate a precision gauge; buy OEM/calibrated. (b) replacement CAM FOLLOWER — it rides the cam profile and participates in needle timing, so it FAILS (ii)/(iii): CORE, never home-made. (c) 3D-printed CARRIER BRACKET THAT TOUCHES THE YARN PATH — because it touches yarn-path registration it FAILS (ii): NOT safe as printed; a bracket that merely holds a cover or a sensor and touches no yarn path and no timing is periphery-OK. So the rule DOES decide these once the 'does it feed stitch-forming metrology/timing?' test is added. GAP: that conjunctive test is NOT written in my spec/KB; as literally worded, the rule is a slogan-plus-two-lists and would let an optimistic builder mis-file a 'bracket' or a 'gauge' as periphery. This is a real operational hole in an owned deliverable.
answers.gap_note: The periphery-vs-core rule lacks an explicit decision test for mechanically-adjacent parts; as written it is two lists. The correct test (does the part set/hold stitch-forming precision — bed flatness, gauge pitch, needle timing, cam geometry, yarn-path registration — or clone firmware/CAD? if yes it is CORE) is derivable and I applied it, but it is not stated. Candidate fix: add the conjunctive 'metrology/timing/yarn-path/IP' test to the periphery-only rule so it adjudicates borderline parts, not just the two canonical lists.
